name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Tuesday 6 June 1972

clue.text: Utile room for privacy here

definitions.note: the answer here is the adjective 'closet', meaning private or secret

blocks.note: first meaning: a small useful room or cupboard for storing things
second meaning: as an adjective it means kept private or secret

explanation.surface: A practical little room in the house offers somewhere to be alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Utile' is an old word for useful.
explanation.definitionFit: A closet is a small storage room, and as an adjective the word describes something kept private, as in a closet drinker.

clue.text: A Prime Minister without his patron saints

definitions.note: the clue defines the full name; the answer is what is left of it

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the following name is taken away from the statesman's full name

blocks.note: David Lloyd George, British Prime Minister 1916-22
St George is the patron saint of England

explanation.surface: A premier is stripped of the saints he was named after.
explanation.walkthrough: Lloyd George's surname contains the name of England's patron saint; take George away and LLOYD is left.
explanation.definitionFit: The remaining word is the first half of the double-barrelled surname of a wartime British premier.

clue.text: But a swan with a pen is no such bird

definitions.text: But a swan with a pen is no such bird

blocks.note: surface reading: a pen is a female swan, so a swan with a pen is just a pair of swans
setter's reading: an office worker holding a writing pen shares a name with an African bird of prey with quill-like crest feathers

explanation.surface: A swan with its mate is unlike a certain other bird.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird is named for its crest feathers, which look like quill pens tucked behind an office clerk's ear.
explanation.definitionFit: The secretary bird is a long-legged African raptor, and a secretary is an office worker who writes with a pen.

clue.text: Steals fabricated tuft of thread

indicators.note: something fabricated is made up or constructed, so the letters are built into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone pinches a piece of trimming made from cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A tassel is a bunch of loose threads bound at one end, hung as ornament on cushions or curtains.

clue.text: Slice of UK cheese

blocks.note: first meaning: a county in north-west England, one piece of the country
second meaning: a crumbly English cheese named after that county

explanation.surface: Someone cuts a piece of British cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slice' looks like it belongs to the cheese, but it means a piece of the map.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheshire is an English county, a region carved out of Britain, and also gives its name to a traditional crumbly cheese.

clue.text: What arc you doing, get ting angry with a rebus?

blocks.note: cross means annoyed or angry
a rebus is a puzzle that spells out words with pictures and letters

explanation.surface: Someone asks why a friend is losing their temper over a picture riddle.
explanation.walkthrough: The scanned clue reads 'arc' for 'are' and splits 'getting'. The opening question is aimed at the solver, who is doing exactly this thing.
explanation.definitionFit: The solver reading the clue is at that moment working on a grid of interlocking clued words, so this is what they are doing.

clue.text: Kipling's thick-skinned gentleman

blocks.note: surface reading: an insensitive man, one who does not take offence easily
setter's reading: a pachyderm from the Just So Stories

explanation.surface: A character from Kipling is a man nobody can offend.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's Just So Stories include 'The Elephant's Child'; thick-skinned is meant literally, as in pachyderm.
explanation.definitionFit: This large African or Asian mammal is a pachyderm, literally thick-skinned, and stars in a famous Kipling story.

clue.text: Time with one nymph in Paradise

blocks.note: an hour is a unit of time
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone spends a while with a beautiful spirit in heaven.
explanation.definitionFit: In Islamic tradition a houri is one of the beautiful maidens who await the faithful in the gardens of Paradise.

clue.text: They're winged and bloody from the knee down

blocks.note: first meaning: wading birds named for their scarlet legs
second meaning: read literally, lower legs coloured blood-red

explanation.surface: Wounded soldiers are hit in the arm and bleeding below the knee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winged' sounds like shot in the arm; here it just means having wings.
explanation.definitionFit: Redshanks are wading birds with bright red legs, and red shanks are literally lower legs coloured crimson.

clue.text: Arden's gold standard?

blocks.note: first meaning: the court jester who follows Rosalind into the Forest of Arden in Shakespeare's As You Like It
second meaning: a dark stone on which gold is rubbed to test its purity, hence any benchmark

explanation.surface: A question about the monetary measure used in Arden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gold standard' looks like economics; it is the stone used to assay gold, and Arden is Shakespeare's forest.
explanation.definitionFit: A touchstone was used to test gold's purity, so it means a benchmark; it is also the clown in As You Like It.

clue.text: Free countries get-together

blocks.note: the United Nations, an organisation of countries
a do is a party or social gathering

explanation.surface: Nations meet without charge.
explanation.definitionFit: To undo a knot or a prisoner's bonds is to free or release them, so the verb is a synonym.

clue.text: Nothing doing here>- on the monster's par?

definitions.text: Nothing doing here>- on the monster's par?

blocks.note: idle means doing nothing
Loch Ness is the monster's home patch

explanation.surface: Nothing is happening by the loch where the monster lives.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan has garbled the punctuation and probably 'patch' or 'pad'; the picture is lazing about on Loch Ness, which is the whole meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Idleness is a state of inactivity where nothing gets done, which is what loafing beside the loch amounts to.

clue.text: Stature of the Southend crew

indicators.note: Southend is in Essex, where speech drops or adds an initial aitch, so the word is judged as spoken there

blocks.note: a rowing crew is an eight; in an aitch-dropping accent the two words are said alike

explanation.surface: A question about how tall the rowers from an Essex seaside town are.
explanation.walkthrough: Southend-on-Sea is an Essex resort; the accent there drops the H, so the rowing word and the measure sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Stature is a person's tallness, and height is the ordinary word for how tall someone stands.

clue.text: Gull sends other birds hack

indicators.note: the scan reads 'hack' for 'back', and sending something back turns it the other way round

blocks.note: auks are diving seabirds such as guillemots and puffins

explanation.surface: A seagull drives other birds away.
explanation.definitionFit: Skuas are piratical seabirds closely related to gulls, sometimes loosely called gulls themselves.

clue.text: Tricks get snake back in side earlier bags

indicators.note: in means the creature is placed inside the other word

blocks.note: knacks are skills or tricks
the snake is an asp; this part of the scan is damaged, and the letters are taken in the order A, P, S
scanning damage: these words seem to have once directed how the snake's letters are ordered, but cannot be read reliably

explanation.surface: Clever tricks let someone sneak a snake into luggage.
explanation.walkthrough: The scanned clue is damaged after 'snake back', so the exact manipulation of the asp is uncertain; the container in tricks is clear.
explanation.definitionFit: Knapsacks are bags carried on the back by hikers and soldiers, so the plural noun fits.

clue.text: Manner to set up for decoration

indicators.note: to set up is to arrange or assemble, so the letters are put into a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fashion is established purely for show.
explanation.definitionFit: An ornament is an object or flourish added for decoration, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Mow one would be served at 71), Simmery Axe

definitions.text: Mow one would be served at 71), Simmery Axe

blocks.note: surface reading: how a customer is attended to at a shop address in the City of London
setter's reading: John Wellington Wells, the sorcerer of Gilbert and Sullivan, deals in magic and spells at No. 70, Simmery Axe

explanation.surface: A question about the service you would get at a certain London shop.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan reads 'Mow' for 'How' and '71)' for '70'. In The Sorcerer, Wells sings that he is a dealer in magic and spells at 70 Simmery Axe, a joke spelling of St Mary Axe.
explanation.definitionFit: At a sorcerer's shop every customer would be attended to by spells and enchantment, so the adverb describes the service.

clue.text: Sort of crab I eat could make me ill

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the noun: these are what could make me ill

indicators.note: to sort is to rearrange, so the following letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A certain shellfish I eat might give me food poisoning.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a complaint about seafood; the germs it fears are the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacteria are microbes, and harmful kinds such as salmonella in bad shellfish cause sickness.

clue.text: Pretty maids all in a row in this state?

definitions.text: Pretty maids all in a row in this state?

blocks.clueFragment: Pretty maids all in a row
blocks.note: surface reading: a line of attractive young women; it is also the last line of the rhyme 'Mary, Mary, quite contrary'
setter's reading: an American state whose name splits as the land belonging to the girl of that nursery rhyme

explanation.surface: A line of pretty girls is found in a certain US state.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme, contrary Mary's garden grows 'pretty maids all in a row', so they grow in Mary's land.
explanation.definitionFit: Maryland is a US state on Chesapeake Bay, and read whimsically it is the land of the nursery-rhyme gardener.

clue.text: Tugs into the wind

indicators.note: turned into something else, the letters change into a new form

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Tugboats head straight into a headwind.
explanation.definitionFit: A gust is a sudden brief rush of wind, so the noun names a burst of moving air.

clue.text: Winding up in flight perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: coiling round and round as it rises
second meaning: a curving flight of stairs, or the corkscrew path of a falling aircraft

explanation.surface: Someone finishes things off while travelling by air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winding up' suggests concluding, and flight suggests aircraft; both point to the coiled shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A spiral is a coiling curve, as in a winding staircase or a plane descending in tight circles.

clue.text: OK. by HM

definitions.note: the answer is a noun or verb meaning agreement

blocks.note: first meaning: agreement or approval
second meaning: the monarch's formal approval that turns a bill into law

explanation.walkthrough: HM is Her Majesty; a bill passed by Parliament becomes law only on receiving royal assent.
explanation.definitionFit: Assent means agreement or consent, and royal assent is the sovereign's formal approval of legislation.

clue.text: One more for shooting?

blocks.note: first meaning: an additional one
second meaning: a background actor hired for filming a scene

explanation.surface: Someone asks for another round of ammunition.
explanation.walkthrough: Shooting suggests guns; in film it means recording a scene, where crowd players are hired.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra is something additional, and also a film walk-on hired for crowd scenes during filming.

clue.text: Started to settle in, having been made a lone wolf?

definitions.text: having been made a lone wolf

blocks.note: first meaning: took belongings out of the cases on arrival

blocks.clueFragment: having been made a lone wolf
blocks.note: second meaning: read as ..., removed from the pack

explanation.surface: Someone moving into new surroundings finds themselves isolated.
explanation.walkthrough: A wolf without a pack has been, comically, un-packed.
explanation.definitionFit: On arrival you empty your suitcases to settle in, and a wolf expelled from its pack has literally lost its pack.

clue.text: The slop-light that is up is down

definitions.note: the bird stands for its down, as in eiderdown

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the phrase before it is read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for that is
der is German for the; the rest of this fragment is scanning damage, probably once marking the word as German

explanation.surface: A lamp turned upward is somehow pointing down.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan has garbled the clue; the readable wordplay is the Latin abbreviation reversed plus German 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a sea duck whose soft breast feathers are the down used to stuff quilts called eiderdowns.

clue.text: The end of the bunny girl?

definitions.text: The end of the bunny girl?

blocks.note: surface reading: a nightclub waitress in a rabbit costume
setter's reading: a rabbit's rear, its short fluffy tail, which the costume copies

explanation.surface: A question about what became of a Playboy club hostess.
explanation.walkthrough: Bunny girls wore a fluffy pom-pom on the costume's rear to mimic a rabbit's tail.
explanation.definitionFit: A scut is the short stubby tail of a rabbit, hare or deer, the bit at the animal's rear.

clue.text: Sharp operator against cut-throat competition

blocks.note: surface reading: a shrewd businessman in a ruthless market
setter's reading: a thin shaving edge for safety razors, the rival of the open cut-throat razor

explanation.surface: A shrewd dealer battles a ruthless market.
explanation.walkthrough: A cut-throat is an old-fashioned open razor; the disposable edge competes with it for the shaving market.
explanation.definitionFit: This thin steel shaving edge is a literal sharp thing that does its work, and it displaced the cut-throat razor.

clue.text: Adventurous play deploying the spade ace

indicators.note: deploying means spreading out and positioning, so the letters are redistributed

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A bold card game in which the ace of spades is played.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapade is a daring or reckless adventure, a bit of mischievous fun, so it fits adventurous play.

clue.text: Money 1— troubled years for depositors

indicators.note: troubled means disturbed or stirred up, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: the scan reads '1—' for the pound sign; L stands for pound, from Latin libra
taken as written

explanation.surface: Bank customers have had hard years with their money.
explanation.walkthrough: Depositors looks like bank savers; here it means hens, which deposit eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: Laying hens are called layers because they deposit eggs, so these egg producers are depositors.
